walkthroughs.body_html:
Practical Techniques — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Practical Techniques brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Practical Techniques.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A car travels 4 km north then 3 km east. What is its displacement magnitude?
options: 7 km
5 km
1 km
25 km

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
options: Acceleration
Momentum
Kinetic energy
Weight

mcqs.q: What is the difference between brittle and ductile materials?
options: Brittle materials fracture with little or no plastic deformation; ductile materials undergo significant plastic deformation before breaking.
Brittle materials are metals and ductile materials are non-metals.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.
Brittle materials are weak and ductile materials are strong.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a fundamental particle: proton, electron, or neutron?
options: All three (proton, electron, neutron) are fundamental particles that cannot be broken down.
Only the electron — protons and neutrons are made of quarks.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.

mcqs.q: Is radioactive decay periodic — does each nucleus decay at regular intervals?
options: No — decay is a random process; half-life is a statistical property of a large population.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
Yes — each nucleus 'ticks' at intervals of one half-life until it decays.
Brittle materials are metals and ductile materials are non-metals.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vector”?
options: The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Scalar”?
options: Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
